prompt: A work laptop says “Updates failed — 23 days.” What do you do?

choices.label: Ignore it. Updates are IT's problem
Report it to IT through the help desk
Search online for an update tool and run it
Keep clicking Remind me later until it stops

why: Failed updates are something you report, not something you fix with tools from the internet. IT can see why it failed and push the fix safely.

prompt: The security agent icon on your laptop is grey with a line through it. Best move?

choices.label: Turn it back on in settings yourself
Uninstall and reinstall it
Tell IT the agent is off
Leave it. The firewall is enough

why: A security tool that's switched off can mean a fault or tampering. Let IT look at it. Don't toggle security tools on or off yourself.

prompt: You restart the laptop and the same “updates failed” warning comes back. Now what?

choices.label: Restart it again until it works
Report it to IT. A restart that doesn't clear it means something's wrong
Switch to your personal laptop for work
Turn off automatic updates to stop the warning

why: A restart is a fair first try. When the warning survives it, it's an IT problem. Report it.

prompt: Why do missing security updates matter?

choices.label: They slow the laptop down
Attackers target known holes that updates already fixed
They only affect new features
They don't, if you have a strong password

why: Most break-ins use flaws that already have a fix. An unpatched machine is an open window.

prompt: A pop-up in your browser says your software is out of date and offers a download. What do you do?

choices.label: Click it. It's helping
Close it, and report it if it keeps showing up. Updates come from IT's own tools
Download it, but scan it first
Forward the link to a coworker to check

why: Fake update prompts are a common way to deliver malware. Real updates come through IT's managed tools.

prompt: Who should you tell when a work device stops updating?

choices.label: Nobody, it will fix itself
A coworker who is good with computers
IT, using the help desk number on your badge
The device maker's support line

why: Use the official help desk contact you already have. IT owns the fix and the record.

prompt: Your phone shows “New sign-in to your account from Reno, NV. Was this you?” You're at your desk in the office. What do you do?

choices.label: Tap Yes so it stops bugging you
Ignore it
Tap No, then report it to security
Change your phone's lock screen

why: A sign-in you didn't make means someone may have your password. Deny it and report it right away.

prompt: You swiped away a sign-in alert you didn't trigger. What's the risk?

choices.label: None, swiping it away blocks it
The session may stay open, and nobody knows to stop it
Your phone battery runs down
Only that you'll get another alert

why: Dismissing isn't denying. Security can only shut down what they know about.

prompt: Ten approve-sign-in prompts hit your phone in a row at 1 a.m. What does that usually mean?

choices.label: The app is glitching
Someone has your password and hopes you tap Approve
IT is testing the system
Your phone needs an update

why: Prompt bombing tries to wear you down. Approve nothing you didn't start, and report it.

prompt: Where should you report an unexpected sign-in alert?

choices.label: Reply to the alert email
Security, at the number or address you already know
Post in the team chat
Wait and mention it at the next team meeting

why: Use a channel you already trust, not one from the alert. Report it as soon as you see it.

prompt: An alert says someone signed in from your usual city, but at a time you were asleep. What do you do?

choices.label: Nothing, the city matches
Report it. The time doesn't fit, so it wasn't you
Sign in yourself to check it's still working
Delete the alert

why: Any sign-in you didn't make is worth reporting, even if the location looks normal.

prompt: After you report a strange sign-in, what will security most likely do?

choices.label: Blame you for the breach
End the session and help you reset your password
Nothing until next week
Ask you to approve it to see who it is

why: Fast reports let security cut the session off and reset access before damage is done. Reporting isn't admitting fault.

prompt: You type “Mark” and autocomplete fills in an address. Before you send a file with customer data, you should

choices.label: Trust autocomplete. It's usually right
Check the full address in the To line
Add more people so the right Mark gets it
Send it and ask Mark if he got it

why: Autocomplete guesses. Read the whole address, especially when it says external.

prompt: You just sent a customer list to the wrong person outside the company. What's the right move?

choices.label: Delete it from Sent and hope nobody notices
Report it to security right away
Email the person asking them to ignore it
Wait to see if they reply

why: Fast reporting gives security the best chance to recall it and handle notice. Hiding it makes it worse.

prompt: Which is an unintentional data exposure?

choices.label: Locking your screen
Sharing a file with an “anyone with the link” setting
Using the shred bin
Calling the help desk

why: Open share links travel far beyond the people you meant. Share only with named people.

prompt: You want a chatbot to summarize a spreadsheet of customer names and addresses. What do you do?

choices.label: Paste it into a public AI tool
Use only the tools your company has approved for that data, or don't paste it at all
Paste half of it
Paste it, then delete the chat

why: Data pasted into a public tool has left the company. Use approved tools or leave customer data out.

prompt: An “external” tag appears next to a recipient name. What is it telling you?

choices.label: The person is a VIP
The address is outside the company. Double-check before sending
The email will be encrypted
Nothing important

why: The external tag is your last warning before data leaves. Stop and check.

prompt: Why does it matter whether a misdirected email is reported in minutes or in days?

choices.label: It doesn't, the data is gone either way
Quick reports can allow a recall and keep the exposure small
Only managers can report it
Reports are only needed for paper

why: Speed is what limits the damage. Mistakes happen; hiding them is what turns them into incidents.

prompt: You're leaving for the night. A printout with customer data is still on the printer. What do you do?

choices.label: Leave it for the morning
Put it in the paper recycling bin
Put it in the locked shred bin
Take it home to finish later

why: Confidential paper goes in the locked shred console, never the recycling or your bag.

prompt: You step away from your desk for two minutes. Your screen should be

choices.label: Left on so you don't lose your place
Locked
Turned to face the wall
Dimmed

why: Lock it every time you stand up. Two minutes is long enough for someone to use it.

prompt: Where should you keep a work password?

choices.label: On a sticky note under the keyboard
In the company password manager
In a note on your phone
In your head and on the monitor as a backup

why: A password manager keeps it safe and lets you use long, unique passwords. Sticky notes are readable by anyone walking by.

prompt: You find a coworker's password on a sticky note on their monitor. Best move?

choices.label: Leave it, it's their business
Remove it and let them or IT know, so it gets changed
Take a photo of it as proof
Try it to see if it works

why: Take it off display and tell them or IT. Once a password has been out in the open, it should be changed.

prompt: Is it OK to take customer printouts home to finish your work?

choices.label: Yes, if you bring them back
Only in a folder
No. Customer data stays in the building unless policy says otherwise
Yes, if it's after hours

why: Paper outside the office is easy to lose and hard to track. Keep it in, and shred it when you're done.

prompt: Which bin is right for a page listing customer names and card numbers?

choices.label: General trash
Open paper recycling
Locked secure-shred console
Any bin, if you tear it in half first

why: Only the locked shred console destroys it safely. Torn paper can be pieced back together.
